If the positive odd integer n has prime factorization
n=∏r=1s​prer​​,
(1)
its Jacobi symbol is
(na​)=∏r=1s​(pr​a​)er​,
(2)
where each factor is a Legendre symbol; by convention (a/1)=1. Thus the symbol is zero exactly when gcd(a,n)>1.
The quadratic reciprocity law for the Jacobi symbol says that for coprime positive odd integers m,n,
(nm​)(mn​)=(−1)(m−1)(n−1)/4.​
(3)
To prove it, write m=∏i​piei​​ and n=∏j​qjfj​​. The quadratic reciprocity law for distinct odd primes states
(qj​pi​​)(pi​qj​​)=(−1)(pi​−1)(qj​−1)/4.
(4)
Multiplying this identity over i,j with multiplicities ei​fj​ gives the required product of Jacobi symbols. Its sign exponent modulo two is
(∑i​ei​2pi​−1​)(∑j​fj​2qj​−1​)≡2m−1​2n−1​(mod2),
(5)
because multiplication of odd integers adds the quantities (r−1)/2 modulo two. This proves the law.
For the requested value, two applications of reciprocity give
(2019503​)=−(5037​)=(76​)=−1,
(6)
since 2019≡7(mod503), 503≡6(mod7), and 6 is a quadratic nonresidue modulo 7.

Every Kn​ is contained in the bounded set K1​, so the intersection K=⋂n≥1​Kn​ is bounded. It is closed because an arbitrary intersection of closed sets is closed.
It remains to prove that K is nonempty. Choose xn​∈Kn​. The set K1​ is a compact set, so some subsequence xnj​​ converges to a point x∈K1​. For each fixed m, all sufficiently late terms satisfy nj​≥m and hence xnj​​∈Knj​​⊆Km​. Since Km​ is closed, x∈Km​. This holds for every m, so x∈K. Thus K∈K.

ρ(Kn​,K)=supx∈Kn​​infy∈K​∣x−y∣.

infy∈K​∣xj​−y∣≥ε.

3G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 180 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 180
3G OurBigBook.com
Let n=2l−1 and let H be the l×n parity-check matrix whose columns are the distinct nonzero vectors of the finite field vector space F2l​. The binary Hamming code is
C=kerH={x∈F2n​:HxT=0}.
(10)
A perfect code has Hamming balls of radius t=⌊(d−1)/2⌋ about its codewords partitioning the whole ambient space, where d is its minimum Hamming distance of a linear code.
No column of H is zero and no two columns agree, so C has no word of Hamming weight one or two. Three suitable columns sum to zero, so d=3. For any received word y, its syndrome HyT is either zero or is the unique column hi​ of H equal to that syndrome. In the first case y∈C; in the second,
H(y+ei​)T=HyT+hi​=0,
(11)
so y is at Hamming distance one from a codeword. Uniqueness follows from d=3. Thus the radius-one balls partition F2n​, and the code is perfect.
For l=3, the dual code is the binary simplex code of length seven. Every nonzero dual word evaluates a nonzero linear functional on the seven nonzero vectors of F23​, and exactly four of those evaluations are one. Hence every nonzero word of C⊥ has weight
4​.
(12)

4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 113
a OurBigBook.com
A recursive set E⊆N0​ has an indicator function computed by a register machine that halts on every input. A recursively enumerable set is the exact halting set of some register machine; equivalently, it is the domain of a partial computable function.
If E is recursive, its decider immediately gives machines that halt exactly on E and on N0​∖E, so both sets are recursively enumerable. Conversely, suppose machines ME​ and MEc​ recognize the two sets. On input x, use dovetailing to run one step of ME​(x) and one step of MEc​(x) alternately. Exactly one must eventually halt. Return one if ME​ halts first and zero if MEc​ halts first. This is a total decider for E, so E is recursive.

b OurBigBook.com
Encode each k-tuple of nonnegative integers by one nonnegative integer using a computable pairing function. Define a unary partial procedure P on input m as follows: use dovetailing on the computations of fn,k​ over all encoded k-tuples, and halt as soon as one of them halts with output m. Then
P(m)↓⟺∃(m1​,…,mk​)∈N0k​:fn,k​(m1​,…,mk​)=m.
(13)
By the Church–Turing thesis, this effective procedure is implemented by a register machine with some fixed code j, so
E={m∈N0​:fj,1​(m)↓}.
(14)
Thus E is the domain of a partial computable function and is recursively enumerable.

The function is the predecessor function. It has the primitive recursion definition
f(0)=0,f(n+1)=n.
(15)
The initial function is the zero function and the recursion step is a projection function, both of which are primitive recursive functions. Closure under primitive recursion therefore proves that f is primitive recursive.

5J (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 212 Articles: 4
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 99 Articles: 1
5J OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 99
a OurBigBook.com
For participants with the same recorded history, the first linear regression estimates that one additional average mile cycled per week is associated with 0.04917 fewer asthma episodes. The corresponding p-value is 0.00761, giving evidence against a zero conditional association.
The second model estimates that, among participants with the same history, receiving the incentive is associated with 0.91387 more episodes. The third estimates that receiving the incentive is associated with 1.73282 more miles cycled per week. Both incentive coefficients have very small p-values. Because the incentive was assigned in a randomized controlled trial, these last two comparisons estimate a causal effect of the incentive.

b

Words: 113 Articles: 1
5J OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 113
b OurBigBook.com
The first model alone would suggest that more cycling is beneficial, but cycling was not randomized in that model: its coefficient can be distorted by confounding or reverse causality. The randomized incentive both substantially increased cycling and substantially increased asthma episodes.
If the incentive affects asthma only through cycling, it is an instrumental variable, and the corresponding Wald estimator of the effect per additional weekly mile is
1.732820.91387​≈0.527
(16)
additional episodes. Under that exclusion assumption the evidence therefore advises against cycling to work more often for this population. Without the exclusion assumption, the experiment establishes the harmful effect of the incentive itself but cannot by itself distinguish an effect of cycling from a direct effect of the monetary incentive.

uv2=a,v−uv2=0,

J=(a2−a2​2−1​),trJ=a2−1,detJ=a2.

The linear stability analysis of a two-dimensional system requires negative trace and positive determinant. Since a>0, the homogeneous equilibrium is stable exactly when
0<a<1​.

Jq​=J−q(D0​01​).

Apply the residue theorem to the upper-half-plane semicircle, with a small semicircular indentation above the pole at z=0. The large arc contributes zero because f(z)/z→0, so
z(z2+a2)f(z)​=o(∣z∣−2).
(25)
The small indentation is traversed clockwise and contributes −iπ times the residue at zero. The only pole strictly inside the indented contour is z=ia. Therefore
PV∫−∞∞​x(x2+a2)f(x)​dx=2πiResz=ia​z(z2+a2)f(z)​+iπResz=0​z(z2+a2)f(z)​.
(26)
The two residues are
Resz=ia​=−2a2f(ia)​,Resz=0​=a2f(0)​.
(27)
Consequently the Cauchy principal value is
PV∫−∞∞​x(x2+a2)f(x)​dx=a2iπ​(f(0)−f(ia)).​
(28)

For each position i, Alice uses yi​ to choose a basis and xi​ to choose a vector in that basis. Explicitly, she sends the qubit
∣ψi​⟩=Hyi​∣xi​⟩.
(43)
Thus yi​=0 uses the computational basis {∣0⟩,∣1⟩}, while yi​=1 uses the Hadamard basis {∣+⟩,∣−⟩}.

b

Words: 103 Articles: 1
10D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 103
b OurBigBook.com
Alice sends the m conjugate-coded qubits through the noiseless quantum channel. Bob independently chooses a uniformly random basis bit yi′​ for each qubit and performs a projective measurement in the computational basis when yi′​=0 or the Hadamard basis when yi′​=1.
After all measurements, Alice and Bob publicly reveal Y and Y′ but keep the data bits secret. They discard every position with yi​=yi′​ and retain the measured bits at positions where the bases agree. In the ideal channel those retained bits equal Alice's xi​ with certainty. Each pair of bases agrees with probability 1/2, so the shared secret key has expected length m/2.

c

Words: 74 Articles: 1
10D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 74
c OurBigBook.com
Condition on a position retained after basis reconciliation, so Bob used Alice's basis. If Eve does not intercept, no error occurs. If she intercepts, her uniformly chosen basis agrees with Alice's with probability 1/2, again causing no error. With probability 1/2 she uses the conjugate basis; her measurement and resent state then make Bob's bit uniformly random, giving an error with probability 1/2.
Therefore the bit error rate in the retained key is
p×21​×21​=4p​.​
(44)

12G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 272 Articles: 7
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 177
12G OurBigBook.com
The binary Huffman coding algorithm repeatedly merges the two currently least probable symbols into one meta-symbol whose probability is their sum. After recursively constructing a code for the smaller alphabet, append 0 and 1 to the meta-symbol's codeword to obtain codewords for the merged pair. The result is a binary prefix code.
To prove optimality, begin with an optimal prefix-code tree. It may be taken to be full, since an internal vertex with one child can be suppressed and all codewords below it shortened. Two leaves of maximum depth are siblings. By exchanging labels, without changing lengths, assign two least probable symbols to such a sibling pair: moving a smaller probability to a no-shorter codeword cannot increase the expected length. Contracting this pair to one leaf replaces their contribution pi​ℓi​+pj​ℓj​ by (pi​+pj​)(ℓi​−1) plus the constant pi​+pj​. If the contracted code were not optimal for the reduced alphabet, replacing it by a better one and then expanding the merged leaf would improve the original code. Mathematical induction on the number of symbols now proves that the Huffman construction minimizes expected word length.

The inductive definition of ordinal addition is the transfinite recursion
α+0=α,α+(β+1)=(α+β)+1,α+λ=supγ<λ​(α+γ)
(76)
for every nonzero limit ordinal λ. The synthetic definition takes disjoint well-orders A and B of order types α and β, puts every member of A before every member of B, and defines α+β to be the order type of this ordered sum.
These definitions agree by transfinite induction on β. The empty second order contributes nothing; adjoining a greatest element gives the successor clause; and a limit well-order is the union of all of its proper initial segments, so its ordered sum with A has order type supγ<λ​(α+γ).

The statement fails for K5​. Colour the edges of a five-cycle blue and its complementary five-cycle yellow. Neither colour contains a triangle.

The triangle-packing Ramsey number is

If their colour disagrees with the packing already constructed, apply the overlap assertion to an oppositely coloured pair; replacing that pair by the overlapping pair is the augmenting move that shifts the boundary between the two packings. Repeating the move either adds a triangle to the existing colour or converts all pairs needed for the opposite-colour packing. Every blue triangle uses at least two vertices of B1​∪B2​, and t such triangles would require a blue perfect matching on those 2t vertices, impossible because the isolated one-vertex blue component B1​ and the odd component B2​ have no such matching. Let ζ be a primitive fifth root of unity. Over Fp​, the Frobenius automorphism acts by ζ↦ζp, so the splitting field of X5−1 has degree equal to the multiplicative order of p modulo 5. Its Galois group is generated by Frobenius and is cyclic. The possible orders are therefore 1 for p≡1, 4 for p≡2,3, and 2 for p≡4(mod5).
Put α=51/5. The polynomial X5−5 satisfies the Eisenstein criterion at 5, so [Q(α):Q]=5. Also [Q(ζ):Q]=φ(5)=4. The intersection of these two fields has degree dividing both 5 and 4, hence is Q. Since the splitting field is Q(α,ζ),
[Q(α,ζ):Q]=20.​
(85)
Label the five roots by αζi, i∈F5​. The Galois group acts through the affine group over a finite field:
i⟼ai+b,a∈F5×​,b∈F5​.
(86)
Its possible nontrivial cycle types are 5, 1+2+2, and 1+4; in particular, no element has a three-cycle. By the Dedekind factorization cycle test, the reduction of X5−5 modulo any prime p=5 therefore has no irreducible cubic factor.
The multiplier of the Frobenius element is a=p(mod5). If p≡2 or 3, then a has order four; every affine map with this multiplier has one fixed point and one four-cycle. Hence X5−5 is a product of a linear factor and an irreducible quartic. If p≡1, Frobenius is a translation i↦i+b: it is the identity when b=0, giving complete splitting, and is a five-cycle when b=0, giving an irreducible polynomial.

View infinity as the puncture of the Riemann sphere and consider g(1/z) near z=0. If this map had an essential singularity, the Great Picard theorem in a coordinate chart would make almost every nearby value occur infinitely often, contradicting the injectivity of g. The singularity is therefore removable as a map into the compact Riemann surface R, and g extends to a nonconstant holomorphic map
g​:P1⟶R.
(119)
The extension is injective. A collision between g​(∞) and g(z0​), or local degree greater than one at infinity, would give nearby values two distinct preimages by the local normal form of a nonconstant holomorphic map, again contradicting injectivity on C. Thus g​ is a holomorphic bijection between compact Riemann surfaces and hence a biholomorphism. Therefore R≅P1, whose genus is zero.

31E (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 249 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 249
31E OurBigBook.com
A map is Devaney-chaotic on Λ when it is topologically transitive, it has dense periodic points in Λ, and it has sensitive dependence on initial conditions. A one-dimensional map is Glendinning-chaotic when some iterate has a horseshoe for an interval map: there are an interval J and two disjoint subintervals K0​,K1​⊆J such that Fn(K0​)=Fn(K1​)=J.
The map F(x)=ax(mod1) is the beta transformation with slope a>1. On every interval of continuity of Fn, it is affine with slope an. The endpoints of these intervals are iterated preimages of the discontinuity set. Choosing n with an>2, the standard full-branch lemma for the beta transformation supplies two disjoint continuity intervals K0​,K1​ on which Fn maps bijectively onto [0,1). Thus Fn has a horseshoe, proving Glendinning chaos.
For Devaney chaos one may either use the standard theorem that a full-branch expanding interval map is Devaney-chaotic, or verify its ingredients directly. Every nonempty open interval expands by the factor a on each uninterrupted iterate; after subdivision at preimages of discontinuities, one of its images contains a full branch and hence eventually covers [0,1). This proves topological transitivity. Applying an inverse branch of a sufficiently high iterate to a full branch gives a contraction whose unique fixed point is periodic; choosing the branch inside any prescribed open interval proves that periodic points are dense. Finally, two sufficiently close points that follow the same branch separate by the factor a on each iterate until their distance exceeds a fixed positive constant, proving sensitive dependence. Hence F is also Devaney-chaotic for every real a>1.

34B (Applications of Quantum Mechanics)

Words: 190 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 190
34B OurBigBook.com
For a normalized trial state ψ, expand it in an orthonormal basis of energy eigenstates, ψ=∑n​cn​ψn​. The Rayleigh quotient is then
⟨H⟩ψ​=∑n​∣cn​∣2En​≥E0​∑n​∣cn​∣2=E0​.
(200)
This is the quantum variational principle: minimizing the expectation of the Hamiltonian operator over any trial family gives an upper bound on the ground-state energy.
Let ψ be the normalized ground-state wavefunction and form the normalized dilation ψλ​(x)=λ1/2ψ(λx). Its kinetic and potential expectations are
T(λ)=λ2T,V(λ)=λ−nV.
(201)
The true ground state makes the energy stationary at λ=1, so
0=dλd​(λ2T+λ−nV)​λ=1​=2T−nV.
(202)
Thus the power-law quantum virial theorem gives
2⟨T⟩0​=n⟨V⟩0​.​
(203)
If n≤−3 and A>0, the two sides have opposite signs, because T>0 and V>0. If A<0, the scaled energy λ2T+λ−nV tends to −∞ as λ→∞, since −n>2, so the Hamiltonian is not bounded below. If A=0, the free particle has no normalizable ground state. Hence there is no normalizable ground state for n≤−3.
For n=1 take the normalized Gaussian function
ψα​(x)=(π2α2​)1/4e−α2x2.
(204)
The Gaussian integral gives
⟨T⟩α​=2mℏ2α2​,⟨∣x∣⟩α​=2π​α1​,
(205)
and therefore
E(α)=2mℏ2α2​+2π​αA​.
(206)
Its unique minimum satisfies
α3=2π​ℏ2mA​.
(207)
At this point ⟨V⟩=2⟨T⟩, consistently with the virial theorem, and the resulting variational estimate is
E0​≤23​(2πmA2ℏ2​)1/3.​
(208)

35D (Statistical Physics)

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 131
35D OurBigBook.com
For one molecule whose translational motion separates from its internal degrees of freedom, the classical one-particle partition function is
z1​(T,V)=λ3V​qint​(T),λ=mkB​T2πℏ2​​,
(209)
where qint​ contains rotational, vibrational, and other internal states. For N indistinguishable noninteracting molecules, the classical ideal-gas partition function is ZN​=z1N​/N!. The thermodynamic pressure therefore obeys
P=kB​T(∂V∂logZN​​)T,N​=VNkB​T​,
(210)
so
PV=NkB​T.​
(211)
The internal structure changes the energy, entropy, and heat capacity through qint​(T), but it does not change the ideal gas law while the internal partition function is independent of volume and the molecules have negligible interactions.
For a dilute monatomic gas qint​=1. Using the Stirling formula in ZN​=(V/λ3)N/N! and differentiating the Helmholtz free energy F=−kB​TlogZN​ gives the Sackur-Tetrode equation
S=NkB​[log(NV​(h22πmkB​T​)3/2)+25​].​
(212)
With N fixed, an isentropic process therefore satisfies VT3/2=constant, or TV2/3=constant. Eliminating T with the ideal-gas law yields the monatomic reversible ideal-gas adiabat
PV5/3=constant.​
(213)
